title: UAPA Detainee Spends 900 Days in Jail Without Trial — Family Says He Was Picked Up 'For Reading'
subtitle: Mohammad Aamir Khan, a schoolteacher from Muzaffarnagar, has been held under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act since October 2023. His bail hearings have been postponed eleven times.
excerpt: A UP schoolteacher arrested under UAPA in 2023 has spent over 900 days in judicial custody without a single day of trial. His wife, who works as a domestic worker to feed their three children, says the only evidence she has seen is a list of books found in their home.
body:
The Arrest

On the night of October 14, 2023, a team of Uttar Pradesh Police and National Investigation Agency officers arrived at Mohammad Aamir Khan's home in Muzaffarnagar's Budhana tehsil. His wife, Rukhsana Begum, says they did not show a warrant. By morning, her husband — a government school teacher with eighteen years of service — was gone.

Nine hundred and twelve days later, he has still not stood trial.

What the Chargesheet Says

The chargesheet, filed six months after the arrest, lists possession of 'seditious literature' and 'suspected links to a banned organisation' as the primary charges. When The Asr reviewed the document, the literature in question included two books on the history of the Partition and a Urdu poetry collection by Faiz Ahmed Faiz.

'He was a reader,' Rukhsana told us during a visit to their home in Budhana. 'Every teacher reads. Is that a crime now?'

Eleven Postponed Hearings

Court records accessed by The Asr show that bail hearings in the case have been adjourned eleven times since November 2023 — six times because the prosecution requested more time, three times due to procedural delays, and twice because the designated Special NIA Court in Lucknow was hearing other cases.

His lawyer, who asked not to be named citing fear of professional consequences, described the situation as 'a system designed to punish through process.'

The bail hearing itself has become the punishment. By the time any court looks at the merits, years have passed and the family has collapsed.

A Family Surviving

Rukhsana now works six days a week cleaning homes in a nearby colony. Their eldest daughter, sixteen, dropped out of school last year to care for her younger siblings. The family's savings are exhausted. A relative crowdfunded Rs 40,000 for legal fees, which ran out after the third hearing.

The Asr sent detailed questions to the UP Police's media cell and the NIA's press officer. Neither responded before publication.

featuredImage.caption: An empty sessions court. Aamir's bail hearing has been postponed eleven times.

seo.metaTitle: UAPA Detainee Held 900 Days Without Trial in Muzaffarnagar
seo.metaDescription: Mohammad Aamir Khan, a UP schoolteacher arrested under UAPA in 2023, has spent over 900 days in custody without trial. His bail hearings have been postponed eleven times.

title: In Mewat, a Clinic Closes and No One Comes to Replace It
subtitle: The only government health centre serving 14 villages in Haryana's Nuh district shut down in March after its sole doctor was transferred. Four months on, the post remains vacant.
excerpt: When the district's only PHC doctor was transferred in March, residents of 14 villages in Mewat lost access to basic maternal care, vaccinations, and tuberculosis treatment. Four months later, no replacement has been posted.
body:
On a Thursday morning in late May, Fatima Khatun walked four kilometres with her seven-month-old daughter to reach the Primary Health Centre at Tauru in Haryana's Nuh district — only to find it locked. A handwritten note on the door read: Doctor unavailable. Visit district hospital.

The district hospital is 34 kilometres away. Fatima does not own a vehicle. The bus runs twice a day.

One Doctor, Fourteen Villages

The Tauru PHC was the sole government medical facility serving a cluster of fourteen villages with a combined population of approximately 38,000 people, the majority of whom are from the Meo Muslim community. When Dr Suresh Yadav — its only physician — was transferred to a facility in Gurugram in early March, the centre did not close officially. It simply stopped functioning.

Health department records reviewed by The Asr show that the vacancy has been marked as 'pending appointment' since March 12. No appointment has been made.

What Is Being Missed

Community health workers in the area told The Asr that at least six pregnant women in the cluster are now receiving no antenatal care. The centre's monthly immunisation camp — which typically vaccinated between forty and sixty children — has not been held since February. A tuberculosis patient who had been receiving DOTS treatment at the centre has missed three consecutive doses.

When we asked the ASHA worker what to do, she said go to Nuh. How? My husband is a daily labourer. I cannot spend 200 rupees on a bus on a Tuesday morning. — Fatima Khatun, Tauru village

The Response

The Asr contacted the Nuh District Health Officer, Dr Pradeep Bhardwaj, by phone and WhatsApp. He confirmed the transfer but said posting decisions were made by the state directorate in Panchkula. The state directorate did not respond to our written request for comment.

The Haryana government's health department website lists the Tauru PHC as 'functional.'

featuredImage.caption: The Tauru PHC has been effectively non-functional since March.

seo.metaTitle: Mewat Clinic Closes, 14 Villages Left Without Healthcare — Nuh, Haryana
seo.metaDescription: The only government health centre serving 14 villages in Haryana's Nuh district has been non-functional for four months. Pregnant women are missing antenatal care.

title: RSS Delegation Heads to Washington as India Hate Lab Reports 41% Rise in Anti-Christian Hate Speech
subtitle: The Hindu nationalist organisation's first major Western outreach tour comes as new data shows hate speech events targeting Christians in India rose from 115 in 2024 to 162 in 2025.
excerpt: The RSS has announced diplomatic visits to the United States and Europe to repair its international image. Critics say the tour is 'damage control' as independent researchers document a sharp rise in anti-minority hate speech across India.
body:
India's Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh announced this week that it is sending senior leaders to the United States and several European countries in what the organisation describes as an effort to 'share the true picture of India's civilisational ethos' with international audiences.

The announcement comes weeks after the US Commission on International Religious Freedom named the RSS in its annual report, alleging the organisation has carried out acts of violence against minority communities for decades — a charge the RSS denies.

The Numbers

The India Hate Lab, an independent research group that tracks communal hate speech events, recorded 162 hate speech incidents targeting Christians in 2025, up from 115 in 2024 — a 41 percent increase. Incidents targeting Muslims remained the largest category in the dataset.

'This is not a fringe phenomenon,' said a researcher at the lab who asked not to be named. 'These events are documented, they are public, and they happen at organised gatherings.'

The Organisation's Position

RSS General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale, speaking to foreign journalists in New Delhi, said the organisation had 'nothing to hide' and that international criticism was 'based on motivated misreading of Indian society.' He said the visits were intended to create dialogue, not deflect scrutiny.

The BJP government in New Delhi has consistently rejected international reports on minority rights as 'interference in internal matters.'

Reactions

Rights organisations have described the tour as reputational management ahead of increasing international pressure. 'When an organisation responds to documented violence reports by hiring PR rather than accountability, that tells you something,' said one human rights lawyer based in Delhi.

Church groups in India, several of which have documented attacks on prayer meetings and congregations, said they would be watching the outcome of the visits closely.

seo.metaTitle: RSS Goes to Washington as Anti-Christian Hate Speech Rises 41% in India
seo.metaDescription: The RSS is launching Western lobbying visits as India Hate Lab data shows a 41% rise in hate speech events targeting Christians in 2025.

title: The Waqf Amendment Act: What Changes, What Doesn't, and What Remains Unclear
subtitle: A plain-language guide to the provisions of the Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025, what opposition parties and Muslim organisations have contested, and what courts have so far ruled.
excerpt: The Waqf Amendment Act passed in 2025 made sweeping changes to how Islamic charitable endowments are governed in India. We break down what the law actually says, what has been challenged, and what the courts have decided so far.
body:
What Is a Waqf?

A waqf is an Islamic charitable endowment — property donated by a Muslim individual for religious, educational, or social purposes. Once declared a waqf, the property is considered inalienable: it cannot be sold, gifted, or inherited. India has one of the largest waqf estates in the world, comprising over 800,000 properties across the country.

What the Amendment Changes

The 2025 amendment to the Waqf Act 1995 introduced several significant changes:

  • Government oversight: District Collectors now have authority to conduct surveys of waqf properties and resolve title disputes — a function previously reserved for Waqf Boards.
  • Board composition: Non-Muslim members can now be appointed to State Waqf Boards, which were previously composed entirely of Muslims.
  • User waqf: The amendment removes the concept of 'waqf by user' — the long-standing practice by which a property used for religious purposes over time could be declared a waqf even without a formal deed.
  • Central database: All waqf properties must be entered into a new centrally managed portal within six months.

What Has Been Challenged

Petitions filed before the Supreme Court and several High Courts have contested the amendments on multiple grounds. Petitioners argue that allowing non-Muslim members on Waqf Boards violates the constitutional right of religious minorities to manage their own religious affairs under Article 26. The removal of 'waqf by user' has been challenged as potentially stripping recognised mosques and dargahs of legal status.

Where the Courts Stand

As of May 2026, the Supreme Court has issued notices to the central government in the consolidated petitions but has not stayed the Act. A three-judge bench is scheduled to hear arguments on the constitutional questions in July.

The constitutional question here is precise: does the state have the right to determine the internal governance structures of a religious minority's charitable institutions? That is not settled law in India.

What Remains Unclear

Several practical questions have not been resolved: how disputes between Collectors and Waqf Boards will be adjudicated; what happens to properties currently in litigation that might lose waqf status under the new 'user' provisions; and whether the six-month database deadline will be enforced.

featuredImage.caption: The Supreme Court has issued notices but has not yet stayed the Waqf Amendment Act.

seo.metaTitle: Waqf Amendment Act 2025 Explained: Key Changes, Court Challenges
seo.metaDescription: A plain-language guide to what India's Waqf Amendment Act 2025 actually changes, what has been challenged in court, and what remains unresolved.

title: 'We Were Told to Leave or Be Ready for Consequences' — Dalit Farmers Describe Intimidation in Hathras
subtitle: Seven Dalit families in Uttar Pradesh's Hathras district say dominant-caste landowners have been pressuring them to abandon agricultural land they legally own — and that police have not registered their complaints.
excerpt: Seven Dalit families in Hathras say they have been threatened with violence if they continue to farm their legally-owned land. When they approached police to file an FIR, they were turned away. Two families have already left.
body:
Ramkali, 54, unfolds a yellowed document on her charpoy and smooths it with both hands. It is the patta — the land title certificate — for 1.2 acres in Hathras district, Uttar Pradesh. Her name is on it. Her late husband's name is on it. The land has been in her family since 1987.

She has not been able to farm it since February.

The Threats

Ramkali is one of seven Dalit landowners in the Sadabad tehsil who say they have received escalating threats from members of a dominant-caste landowning family to stop cultivating their plots. Accounts provided to The Asr, gathered over three days of field reporting, describe verbal warnings, the destruction of a crop, and, in one case, a physical altercation in which two men were reportedly beaten.

'They said: leave the land or leave the village. We have been here for forty years. Where do we go?' said Ramkali's son, Suresh Kumar.

Police Did Not Register Complaints

Six of the seven families say they went to the Sadabad police station to register complaints and were turned away. One family was told the matter was 'civil, not criminal.' Another was advised to 'resolve it internally.'

The Asr obtained a copy of one written complaint submitted to the Station House Officer in March. The document bears a receipt stamp but no FIR number — indicating it was received but not registered as a case.

The Sadabad SHO did not respond to calls or messages. The SP Hathras office told The Asr in writing that the matter was 'being looked into.'

A Pattern Researchers Recognise

'What you're describing in Hathras is not unusual,' said a researcher at the National Dalit Movement for Justice, reached by phone. 'In western UP, land disputes involving SC communities and dominant-caste landowners are routinely classified as civil matters by police to avoid SC/ST Act provisions. The refusal to register is itself an offence under the Act.'

Two of the seven families have already relocated to their relatives' homes in a nearby town. Ramkali says she will not leave.

featuredImage.caption: Ramkali's 1.2-acre plot, which she has been unable to farm since February.

seo.metaTitle: Dalit Farmers Threatened Off Their Own Land in Hathras, Police Won't Act
seo.metaDescription: Seven Dalit families in UP's Hathras district report intimidation by dominant-caste landowners. Police have refused to register their complaints.

title: Opinion: The 'Love Jihad' Law Has Not Prevented a Single Marriage. It Has Ended Several Careers.
subtitle: Four years since UP's Unlawful Religious Conversion law came into force, the evidence suggests it is being used not to prevent coercion but to police consensual relationships.
excerpt: UP's anti-conversion law, invoked over 350 times since 2020, was sold as protection for vulnerable women. An analysis of the cases suggests it has functioned primarily as a tool to criminalise interfaith couples and the men who support them.
body:
The Uttar Pradesh Prohibition of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Act, 2021, has been on the books for four years. In that time, the state has invoked it more than 350 times. I have spent the past two months going through the available case records, talking to lawyers who have defended accused persons, and speaking with two women who were identified as the 'victims' in cases — and who say they were not victims of anything.

What the Law Was Supposed to Do

Supporters of the legislation, including the BJP state government that passed it, argued it was necessary to prevent women — particularly Hindu women — from being deceived into religious conversion through fraudulent marriages. The law mandates prison sentences of up to ten years for conversion 'by misrepresentation, force, fraud, undue influence, coercion, allurement or any fraudulent means,' with harsher penalties if the victim is a woman or belongs to a Scheduled Caste or Tribe.

What It Has Actually Done

Of the 350-plus cases reviewed, legal observers and defence lawyers say the overwhelming majority involve complaints filed not by the women in question, but by their male relatives. In many cases, the women have filed affidavits in court asserting that the relationship was consensual and that they did not wish to convert or had done so of their own free will.

Lawyer Farrukh Khan, who has defended twenty-three accused persons under the Act in Allahabad High Court, told me: 'In not one of my cases did the woman come to court saying she had been coerced. In every single case, it was her father or her brother.'

Two Women Speak

Priya (name changed), a 24-year-old from Agra, had been in a relationship with a Muslim man for three years before they married in 2022. Her husband was arrested within a week of the wedding under the Act. She filed an affidavit saying the marriage was her choice.

'The court took my affidavit. The police ignored it. My husband spent eleven months in jail before bail. We are still fighting the case. My in-laws lost their shop because they could not afford to keep up business while managing this.'

A second woman, Ayesha (name changed), converted to Hinduism to marry her partner — and her partner's family filed a complaint anyway. 'The law does not care about women. It cares about keeping communities separate.'

A Tool of Separation

When a law consistently produces outcomes that contradict its stated purpose — when it imprisons men while the women it claims to protect stand in the same court asking for their release — the honest question is whether the purpose was ever what was stated. The evidence in UP suggests the Unlawful Conversion Act functions not as protection but as veto: a mechanism by which a family, a community, or a police officer can override the choices of an adult woman.

Four years in, it has not prevented a single coerced conversion I can find in the record. It has, however, ended several careers, split several families, and imprisoned several men whose partners did not want them imprisoned.

That should be enough to demand a reckoning.

seo.metaTitle: UP's Anti-Conversion Law: Four Years, 350 Cases, No Coercion Found
seo.metaDescription: An analysis of UP's anti-conversion law cases finds it is used overwhelmingly to police consensual relationships — not protect women from coercion.

title: Rohingya Families Describe Conditions in Delhi Detention Centre: 'Children Have Not Seen Sunlight in Weeks'
subtitle: Fifteen Rohingya families, including 23 children, have been held at the Lampur detention facility in outer Delhi since a sweep in January. Advocates say access for legal representatives has been repeatedly denied.
excerpt: Twenty-three Rohingya children are among those detained at Delhi's Lampur facility following January sweeps. Lawyers say they have been denied access for three months, and families report inadequate food, no outdoor access, and a child who was hospitalised.
body:
Through a brief phone call facilitated by an advocacy group, a Rohingya woman detained at Delhi's Lampur detention centre described her family's situation in a few sentences before the call was cut off: 'My children have not gone outside in weeks. My youngest is sick. We don't know what is happening to us.'

She and her husband, along with their four children, have been in the facility since January 17.

The January Sweeps

In the second week of January, Delhi Police and immigration officials conducted a series of coordinated operations across several areas of East and North Delhi, including Madanpur Khadar and Khajuri Khas, where Rohingya refugee communities had been living for years — many with UNHCR documentation.

Human rights groups documented at least 47 individuals taken in the sweeps. Fifteen family units, including 23 children, are believed to still be at Lampur. The rest were deported.

Legal Access Denied

Advocate Priyanka Sharma, who has filed habeas corpus petitions on behalf of seven of the detained families at the Delhi High Court, told The Asr that she has been denied entry to the Lampur facility on three occasions since February.

'I have court orders asking for status reports on my clients. The facility administration has not complied. This is contempt, but it is happening anyway,' she said.

The Delhi High Court has issued notices to the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police. A hearing is scheduled for June.

Conditions Inside

Accounts obtained through phone contact with detainees, and from one family released in March, describe cells with limited ventilation, food described as insufficient and sometimes spoiled, and no access to outdoor space for children. One child, a six-year-old, was taken to hospital in February with what family members were told was a respiratory infection. He was returned to detention after two days.

The Ministry of Home Affairs did not respond to questions submitted in writing. Delhi Police said in a statement that 'all detainees are being held in accordance with applicable law and their welfare is being ensured.'

UNHCR has publicly stated that it is 'concerned about reports of detention of persons of concern.' The agency says it has not been granted access to the facility.

featuredImage.caption: File photo. The Lampur facility has denied access to lawyers and UNHCR.

seo.metaTitle: Rohingya Children Held for Months at Delhi Detention Centre, Lawyers Blocked
seo.metaDescription: 23 Rohingya children are among those held at Delhi's Lampur detention facility since January sweeps. Advocates say legal access has been denied for three months.

title: Madrasa Survey, School Closure: How a UP District Became a Test Case for Education Policy
subtitle: Since a state-ordered survey of madrasas in Bahraich district began in 2024, fifteen institutions have closed or stopped operating. Educators say many were teaching subjects far beyond what critics claim.
excerpt: A state-ordered survey of Bahraich's madrasas has resulted in fifteen closures in eighteen months. When The Asr visited, we found shuttered classrooms, displaced students, and educators who had spent years building something they are now watching disappear.
body:
The madrasa that Maulana Rashid Ahmed built over twenty-two years sits locked behind a rusted gate on the edge of a mustard field in Bahraich's Nanpara tehsil. Inside, according to Ahmed, were classrooms for 340 students, a library of 1,400 books, and a computer lab funded by donations from local traders.

The computer lab was what he was most proud of. 'I wanted these children to have everything,' he said, standing outside the gate. 'Science, mathematics, English, computers. And then the survey came.'

The Survey

In late 2023, the Uttar Pradesh government ordered a district-by-district survey of all madrasas operating in the state, ostensibly to assess their educational standards, infrastructure, and whether they were receiving foreign funding. In Bahraich, a predominantly Muslim district bordering Nepal, 217 madrasas were surveyed.

By May 2026, at least fifteen have shut down. Officials say several were found to be operating without proper registration or with inadequate facilities. Madrasa administrators say the survey process itself — which included unannounced visits and demands for documents on short notice — was designed to find violations rather than assess education.

What the Closed Schools Were Teaching

The Asr visited five of the closed institutions. Across all five, we found evidence of teaching that went beyond traditional religious subjects: student notebooks with algebra problems, science diagrams, and English grammar exercises. Several had NCERTaligned textbooks alongside religious texts.

'They called us medieval. We had a computer lab,' said Ahmed.

The Students

The most concrete impact of the closures has been on students. The Asr spoke with families of 34 children who had been enrolled in now-closed madrasas. Of these, eleven had enrolled in government schools. Nine had stopped formal education altogether. The rest were in transition — waiting to see which nearby institution might accept them.

I don't know what to do with my son now. The government school is three kilometres away and the road is not safe for children. This madrasa was two minutes from my door. — Parent, Nanpara tehsil

The Government's Position

District authorities maintain that closures resulted from genuine violations and that the state has expanded enrolment capacity in government schools to absorb affected students. The UP Madrasa Education Board said in a written statement that 'only non-compliant institutions have been asked to regularise or cease operations.'

featuredImage.caption: One of fifteen madrasas in Bahraich that have ceased operations since 2024.

seo.metaTitle: Madrasa Closures in Bahraich: 15 Shut, Students Displaced — A UP Test Case
seo.metaDescription: Fifteen madrasas in UP's Bahraich district have closed since a state survey began in 2024. The Asr visits shuttered classrooms and speaks to displaced students.

title: She Ran a Ration Shop, Reported Corruption, and Then Received a Lathi: A Dalit Woman's Fight in Rajasthan
subtitle: Kamla Meghwal was one of the first Dalit women to be allocated a fair price shop in her panchayat in Baran district. After she reported grain diversion to the collector, she was assaulted. The man she named was back at work within a month.
excerpt: Kamla Meghwal's ration shop was supposed to be a story about empowerment. Then she reported that a government official was diverting grain, and her shop was cancelled, her complaint was buried, and she was beaten. She is still fighting.
body:
Kamla Meghwal keeps a plastic folder with everything. The original shop allotment letter from 2019. The complaints she filed with the district supply office in 2022. The medical report from the government hospital after the assault in October of that year. The RTI responses — mostly blank or delayed. The FIR that was finally registered six months after the assault, under charges she describes as 'deliberately softened.'

She has been carrying this folder to offices for three years.

How It Started

In 2019, Rajasthan's state government allocated fair price shop licences to women from Scheduled Caste communities as part of a welfare initiative. Kamla, then 38, was one of twelve women in Baran district to receive an allocation. She ran her shop in Kishanganj block, distributing subsidised grains and kerosene to the 200-odd families on her list.

In early 2022, she began noticing discrepancies. The stock she was officially receiving did not match the stock physically arriving at her godown. When she asked the area's grain depot supervisor about the shortfall, she was told the figures were correct and she was mistaken.

She went to the District Supply Officer with documentation of the discrepancy. Then to the Collector. Then she filed an RTI asking for movement records of the grain that should have reached her shop.

What Followed

In October 2022, two men arrived at Kamla's home after dark. Her husband was not present. According to the medical report she showed The Asr, she sustained injuries to her left forearm and shoulder consistent with being struck with a blunt object. She identified one of the men as a relative of the depot supervisor she had complained about.

Her ration shop licence was suspended the following month, ostensibly for 'administrative irregularities.'

The depot supervisor was suspended briefly and reinstated within four weeks. No chargesheet has been filed against him.

Where the Case Stands

An FIR was registered in March 2023 — five months after the assault — naming two men under IPC sections for assault and criminal intimidation. The SC/ST Atrocities Act was not invoked; Kamla's lawyers say this was deliberate. The case has seen three adjournments this year alone.

Kamla's shop licence has not been restored. She now works as a daily wage labourer.

'I did what I was supposed to do,' she said. 'I saw something wrong and I reported it. I did not know this would be my life.'

featuredImage.caption: Kamla Meghwal has been carrying her folder of documents to government offices for three years.

seo.metaTitle: Dalit Ration Shop Owner Reported Corruption, Was Beaten — Rajasthan
seo.metaDescription: Kamla Meghwal reported grain diversion from her ration shop. She was assaulted, her licence was cancelled, and the official she named was reinstated in a month.

title: Sikh Farmers in Punjab's Border Belt Say Canal Water Allocation Has Not Changed in 30 Years — Their Land Has
subtitle: In three villages along the Pakistan border in Gurdaspur district, Sikh farming families describe watching their fields turn saline while downstream areas receive priority water allocation. Officials say the formula is 'equitable.'
excerpt: Sikh farmers in Gurdaspur's border belt have been petitioning for a revision to canal water allocation since the 1990s. Their land has become increasingly saline. The Punjab government says allocation formulas are equitable. The farmers disagree, loudly.
body:
Balwinder Singh grows potatoes on six acres in Dera Baba Nanak block, two kilometres from the Pakistan border. He grows them in soil that is getting harder to grow anything in. 'The water comes for three days. Then it stops for twelve. Then the ground bakes. Then the salts come up.' He holds up a handful of soil. It is pale and crusted.

His neighbours grow the same potatoes on the same schedule and tell the same story. They have been telling it, in varying forms, since at least the mid-1990s.

The Allocation Formula

Punjab's canal water allocation system distributes water from the Ravi-Beas system through a warabandi schedule — a rotational system in which each landowner receives water for a fixed period proportional to their land holding. In principle, this is equitable. In practice, farmers in the Gurdaspur border belt say that the schedule assigned to their villages results in shorter effective irrigation windows because of transmission losses, the distance from headworks, and the priority given to areas with higher crop intensity.

Agricultural department officials in Gurdaspur told The Asr that the warabandi is reviewed periodically and is based on 'scientific assessment of need.' They acknowledged that transmission losses affect water delivery but said this was a 'systemic challenge' affecting all regions.

The Salinity Problem

Soil testing data obtained by The Asr from the Krishi Vigyan Kendra in Gurdaspur shows that electrical conductivity readings — the standard measure of soil salinity — in the three villages visited exceed the threshold for 'moderate salinity stress' in approximately 60 percent of samples from 2024. In 2009, the figure was 22 percent.

Agronomists say the combination of inadequate irrigation and waterlogging from inconsistent supply is a classic driver of salinity build-up in semi-arid border soils.

What Farmers Are Asking

Representatives of the Gurdaspur border belt farmers submitted a memorandum to the Punjab Chief Minister's office in February asking for three things: a revision of the warabandi schedule for border villages, government funding for a drainage improvement project proposed by the agriculture department in 2018 but never implemented, and compensation for yield losses over the past decade.

They received an acknowledgement receipt. No substantive response has followed.

We are not asking for charity. We are asking for what the water schedule owes us. Our grandfathers were given this land by the government after Partition. Now the government is watching it die.

featuredImage.caption: Balwinder Singh's fields in Dera Baba Nanak block, Gurdaspur.

seo.metaTitle: Punjab Border Belt Sikh Farmers Say Canal Water Allocation Has Failed Them
seo.metaDescription: Sikh farmers in Gurdaspur's border belt say unchanged water allocation formulas have driven soil salinity up 38 points in 15 years. The government calls the system equitable.
